title: HTML, Overleaf, and Unleashing the HTML Creator: Reflections on Live Session 2
author: Dr Dario Emanuele
summary: Framed as a follow-up to his second live session, Dario Emanuele's post is a practical guide for teachers to using his custom Gemini Gem, the HTML Creator, to generate classroom resources. He argues that the tool's purpose is to take the heavy lifting out of resource design so teachers can spend their cognitive energy on pedagogy, sequence and responsive teaching. He walks through four resource types built in the session: complete I Do, We Do, You Do learning cycles, interactive worksheets that give students misconception-specific feedback, projectable reveal-style displays, and printable PDF worksheets. He then explains Gemini's new direct download feature and diagnoses the loss of Gemini's live preview, attributing it to Google Drive security blocks and context loss in Gems. He offers two workarounds: generating LaTeX for Overleaf when a publication-quality PDF is needed, and uploading local files instead of Drive-linked knowledge to restore the preview. The footnotes supply his actual prompts and the full system instructions for building a similar Gem.
points: Emanuele positions AI resource generation as a way to offload design work so teachers' cognitive energy goes to pedagogy, sequencing and responsive lesson moves.
Interactive HTML worksheets are shown to deliver immediate, misconception-specific explanations when a student answers wrongly, bringing diagnostic questioning into independent study.
When a polished printable worksheet is the goal, he recommends asking the Gem for LaTeX and compiling it in Overleaf rather than generating HTML.
The missing Gemini preview is traced to security behaviour triggered by Drive-linked knowledge files, fixed by uploading a local copy of the file into the chat instead.
The footnotes provide his full prompt set and Gem system instructions, making the piece a replicable, teacher-specific build guide rather than just a session recap.
quotes: Our main focal point for the session was stretching the capabilities of my custom Gemini Gem, the HTML Creator. The core philosophy of this tool isn’t just to make ‘pretty’ things; it’s to take the heavy lifting out of resource generating and designing so we can focus our precious cognitive energy on pedagogy, sequence, and responsive lesson moves.

We generated digital worksheets where a student can type an answer directly into their screen. If they make a mistake, the HTML code triggers an immediate, responsive explanation detailing why that specific misconception likely occurred and how to rectify it. This brings diagnostic questioning straight to the student’s independent study time.

From there, you simply double-click the file, and it opens instantly in your default web browser (Chrome, Safari, Edge) fully styled, interactive, and completely ready to use or project. It dramatically closes the “knowing-doing” gap for teachers who want to use tech but don’t want to spend ages copy-pasting code behind the scenes.

While it can still write code flawlessly, you can’t always view the final rendered layout within the chat interface before downloading it. This is particularly problematic when you want to make slight adjustments or generate a downloadable PDF straight away; you are essentially flying blind until you export it.

Instead, instruct the Gem to write a fully compliant code structure designed for Overleaf (a free, cloud-based LaTeX editor). LaTeX is unmatched for creating perfectly aligned mathematical equations, tables, and structured grids.

In the final portion of the session, we pulled back the curtain entirely. I don’t just want to hand you the resources; I want you to own the tools. I shared the exact framework and underlying system instructions I used to build the HTML Creator Gem so that you can construct your own custom variant tailored to your subject specialism.
